rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, Tables 1-2 - the authors process their own ASTER and Landsat 7 ETM+ images (2007-2008) for a pilot site near Paphos, apply the FAO Penman-Monteith equation adapted to satellite data to estimate ETc, and compare these with WaterWare model estimates.
rows.notes: The study's own result is a set of daily ETc estimates (2.25-3.03 mm/day) for one pilot area derived from satellite imagery, and a comparison with WaterWare irrigation-demand model values (Table 2). It demonstrates that remote sensing can be used to estimate ETc and thereby monitor irrigation demand; it does not report any result on water policy, scarcity, climate change or competing demands being confronted or managed. The water allocation/optimization component of WaterWare is described but no allocation results are reported (Fig. 5 is only a projection), and the statement that the integration can 'provide scientific data to policy makers' is an assertion in the conclusions, not a finding. The ETc estimates are not validated against ground ET measurements (no lysimeter or flux data; only sun-photometer/spectro-radiometer validation of reflectance). Hence the study supports only a precondition of the claimed effect (monitoring of irrigation demand), not the claimed policy/risk-management effect.

notes: Short pilot-study paper; text appears complete. Results are limited to seven satellite dates in one ~30 km2 pilot area in Paphos, Cyprus, with no dispersion statistics beyond min/max of pixel ETc per image and an approximate 5% atmospheric-correction error.
